title: Radio bursts pin a magnetic field on Beta Pictoris b
freshness: Posted to arXiv as 2609.16720 in September 2026, inside the preferred 15-day freshness window for this daily note.
excerpt: MeerKAT has localized auroral radio bursts to the giant planet Beta Pictoris b, about 20 parsecs away. The emission reaches 3.5 GHz and implies a magnetic field of at least about 1.25 kilogauss, the first direct field-strength measurement for an exoplanet.
whyItMatters: Magnetic fields shape how planets hold atmospheres and how they interact with stellar winds, yet none had been measured directly beyond the Solar System. A confirmed exoplanet with a radio-derived field turns a long-standing model target into an observable, and it opens a path to map fields on other nearby imaged giants.

body:
## A magnetic field you can hear

Planetary magnetic fields matter. They steer atmospheric escape, shape how a planet meets a stellar wind, and leave clues about the metal and rock deep inside. Until now, nobody had measured one directly for a planet beyond the Solar System. Models filled the gap. Direct numbers did not.

The clean signal is auroral radio, the same kind of emission Jupiter and Earth produce when energetic electrons spiral along magnetic field lines. The highest frequency of that emission tracks the field strength at the source. Radio astronomers have caught similar bursts from ultracool dwarfs, and earlier searches of planet-hosting systems either found nothing or could not tell whether the star or the planet was talking. That ambiguity is the problem this result breaks.

## MeerKAT points at Beta Pictoris b

A team led by K. N. Ortiz Ceballos at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, with E. Berger and Y. Cendes, observed the Beta Pictoris system with South Africa's MeerKAT array on four dates in 2025 and 2026, in the L and S bands between about 0.85 and 3.5 GHz. Beta Pictoris sits about 20 parsecs away. The star is roughly 23 million years old, magnetically quiet, and hosts a debris disk plus at least three giant planets. The most massive, Beta Pictoris b, weighs about 12 Jupiter masses and orbits near 10 astronomical units. At its widest, the planet sits about half an arcsecond from the star, far enough for careful radio imaging to separate the two.

They detect a radio source in every epoch. The hard part is ownership. After tying the radio frame to Gaia using nine quasars and one VLBI calibrator, and folding in tests for ionospheric refraction and fitting error, the corrected position matches planet b and conflicts with the host star at about 4.4 sigma and with planet c at about 4.8 sigma. Measured: the radio spot sits on the planet, not the star.

## Bursts that give a field strength

The emission is not a steady hum. It comes as rapid, recurring bursts with circular polarization of about 40 to 70 percent, plus fainter emission between bursts. The polarization and the short timescales point to electron cyclotron maser radiation. Plasma emission would need densities the team finds implausible for a planetary magnetosphere. The S-band burst reaches 3.5 GHz, the top of that observing band, and is also the most polarized. Under the cyclotron-frequency rule, that ceiling requires a magnetic field of at least about 1.25 kilogauss at the emission site. That is the first direct field-strength measurement for an exoplanet. It also sits above the host star's known dipole upper limit of roughly 0.3 kilogauss, another reason the star cannot be the source.

The authors favor magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling, the same rotationally driven engine that powers aurorae at Jupiter and at many ultracool dwarfs. Beta Pictoris b spins in about 8 to 9 hours. An about 8-hour gap between two L-band bursts sits near that period and may be rotational modulation. Stellar-wind driving and an Io-like moon interaction both under-predict the observed power in their checks. Those alternatives are disfavored, not merely left open as equals.

## Why the number travels

Because Beta Pictoris b has a dynamically measured mass, the radio field can be set beside dynamo scaling laws calibrated on Solar System planets and low-mass stars. The planet lands where those laws predict a young, massive giant should sit. Continued monitoring can map magnetic geometry. Seven more nearby directly imaged giants sit at separations where the same localization trick can work, once radio arrays gain about five to seven times more sensitivity.

Caveats belong in the open. The result rests on four observing blocks and on frame-tie systematics that the team inflate on purpose. The paper is an arXiv preprint (2609.16720), so peer review is still ahead. The 1.25 kilogauss figure is a lower limit set by the highest detected frequency, not a full map of the field. Measured: auroral radio, localized to Beta Pictoris b, with a cyclotron ceiling that implies at least about 1.25 kilogauss. Inferred: a working planetary dynamo on a confirmed exoplanet, finally caught in radio light.
